blocks: RESEARCH
Nabokov’s Memory and the Creation of Fictive Authority
Nicholas Anderman
DEPARTMENT OF ENGLISH
Kevin Bell
FACULTY ADVISOR, DEPARTMENT OF ENGLISH, NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

Charles Kinbote, the narrator of Vladimir Nabokov’s 1962 novel Pale Fire, creates fictive authority through the deployment of a selective memory.  The implications of Kinbote’s establishment of power through narrative voice are serious and wide reaching, and ultimately suggest a cultural re-evaluation of the importance of fiction itself.
Introduction

Pale Fire (1962), like much of Russian/American novelist Vladimir Nabokov’s work, brims over with thinly veiled allusion to memories of his own life and other writing.  The novel features Charles Kinbote, a Slavic émigré college professor as narrator, a cameo by Professor Pnin (the subject of Nabokov’s 1957 novel Pnin), and Zembla, a purportedly made-up locale that suggests the Russian arctic island Nova Zembla, where there is a Nabokov River named after the author’s great-grandfather. Nabokov, as a young Russian exile (he fled the country during the Revolution of 1917, when he was 18 years old), understood on a very literal level that those who possess the authority to narrate the past (in the name of an ideological agenda, for example) possess great power indeed.  As his personal and artistic history suggests, Nabokov is very much concerned with the effects of historical representation (and misrepresentation) of the past in the present day.

Scholarly interest in Pale Fire has been and continues to be intense, as the book is rightly considered one of Nabokov’s best and most complex.  Existing Pale Fire scholarship falls into two categories.  There are those like Brian Boyd, major Nabokov scholar and definitive biographer, who view the novel as a puzzle to be solved, citing as motivation for this view Nabokov’s well-known obsession with chess problems.  Others disregard the ‘puzzle’ aspects of the novel in favor of a more inclusive approach, most clearly delineated by Michael Wood, who writes, “what matters is not what happens but what might happen…this is one of the more attractive meanings of ‘fiction.’”ⁱ  Wood hints at the importance of fiction in Pale Fire, but does not go any further.

This paper will argue that in Pale Fire memory, or in Kinbote’s case the calculated distortion of narrative representations of the past, has the effect of drawing attention to the creation of fictive authority itself.  When taken seriously, the idea of memory as a mechanism for composing reality has the potential to challenge the greater epistemological question of how texts possess credibility in the first place.  Pale Fire is an unusually vivid study of a text in the process of dealing with its own authority – a topic vital not only to the study of Nabokov’s entire canon, but also to our collective understanding of history, culture, aesthetics, and politics.
Background

Pale Fire consists of two sections: a nine hundred and ninety-nine line poem called “Pale Fire” by the fairly well-known poet John Shade (“born July 5, 1898, died July 21, 1959”ⁱⁱ), and the commentary on that poem by Dr. Charles Kinbote, a colleague of Shade’s in the English department at Wordsmith College.  Shade’s poem, in five cantos, describes his life and various related themes in rather dated heroic couplets.  The poet’s description of himself as “one oozy footstep”ⁱⁱⁱ behind Robert Frost is apt – much of “Pale Fire” is spent faux-philosophizing on nature, art, death, and the possibility of life after death. Notably, the poem also depicts the death, probably by suicide, of Shade’s only daughter, Hazel.  “Pale Fire” is adorned with a Foreword, extensive commentary, and index, all of which are attributed to the aforementioned Dr. Charles Kinbote.  In addition to their professional link via Wordsmith College, we learn that Kinbote and Shade were neighbors in the Appalachian town of New Wye before Shade’s death.  Kinbote claims to have obtained the rights to the original (and only) copy of “Pale Fire” from Sybil Shade, John’s wife, directly after the poet was gunned to death in Kinbote’s front yard.

Kinbote describes himself as Shade’s best friend, intellectual equal, and ideal editor – identities quickly problematized by Kinbote himself.  From the first page of Pale Fire, it is clear that Kinbote is not a very reliable commentator.  In the Foreword, we learn that he gained the rights to the poem “Pale Fire” under extremely questionable circumstances, and that his coworkers in the English department have serious (and well-founded) doubts about his abilities as an editor.  We learn, alarmingly, that during the “few months”ⁱᵛ he actually knew Shade he often spied on the poet and his wife through the windows of their house.  It is clear from the Foreword that Kinbote’s relationship with Shade was creepy, to put it mildly.  It is also clear that Kinbote himself is an interesting and multi-faceted character.  He informs us that he is a strict vegetarian, drives a “powerful red car,”ᵛ is probably a homosexual, and most perplexingly, believes himself to be the deposed king of a far-away nation called Zembla.

The absurdity of Kinbote’s self-centered Foreword is only expanded upon in his 228 pages of commentary to Shade’s poem.  Each of his comments is attached to a line of “Pale Fire,” but often they do not relate to the subject matter of the poem at all.  Instead, Kinbote uses the comments to narrate what we eventually understand to be the primary plot of Nabokov’s novel:  Kinbote, i.e. King Charles the Beloved, is the recently overthrown king of Zembla, a “distant northern land”ᵛⁱ somewhere in the vicinity of Russia.  He describes in great detail his idyllic royal childhood, his daring escape from Communist-controlled Zembla in 1958, and his ensuing undercover life as a mild-mannered, if eccentric, professor of literature at Wordsmith College in New Wye, Appalachia.  His admiration for Shade’s poetry originated in his youth, and seems to be genuine, albeit misguided.  With this royal framework in place, Kinbote claims that Shade was accidentally shot by the Zemblan assassin Jakob Gradus, whose actual target was the disguised King.  The other explanation for Shade’s murder, seen clearly only after the careful reader pieces together seemingly random facts found throughout Pale Fire, is that Gradus was actually Jack Grey, an escaped convict seeking revenge upon the judge that sentenced him to life in prison.  Shade, we learn, greatly resembles Judge Goldsworth, whose house Kinbote is renting while the judge is on sabbatical in England.  Kinbote, who claims to have visited and talked to Gradus/Grey in prison after the murder, vehemently denies this second explanation, though by the end of the novel Kinbote’s narrative voice has been brought into question too many times to count.

Pale Fire is a confusing read, to say the least. Kinbote’s narration is so obviously flawed as to be hilariously funny at times, and quite unnerving all the time. Ultimately, it is up to the individual reader to decide what to believe.  Zembla, we learn from Kinbote’s coworkers (including Shade himself), is a real place in the world of the book.  This paper works from the position that Kinbote’s explanation of Shade’s murder (and indeed Kinbote’s self-identification as King Charles) is a function of Kinbote’s flawed memory, and so is false.  More importantly, the identification of some concrete “reality” in Pale Fire is not the most fruitful of tasks, as we will eventually see here.  The fact of the matter is, Kinbote’s narration is imperfect, but it is the only narration we have. King Charles the Beloved himself best describes his own treatment of Shade’s poem, when he writes, “…for better or worse, it is the commentator who has the last word.”ᵛⁱⁱ Whether we like it or not, Kinbote’s interpretation of “Pale Fire” is the one we have in front of us, and so must be treated with some modicum of respect.
Memory and Narrative

Kinbote’s flaws as a narrator can be traced to his seriously inconsistent memory.  The term “memory” is used broadly here.  Importantly, the word does not imply anything about the question of intentionality in Kinbote’s professed memories.  Whether or not his misrepresentations of his own history are deliberate – that is, whether or not he is lying to us – is irrelevant.  The fact of the matter is, Kinbote actively and often distorts the past, and it is impossible to know his precise motives.  In this paper, then, the term “memory” is used to refer to any and all of Kinbote’s narrative distortions.  This admittedly broad view of the narration of Pale Fire is possible only because the book is a flashback, related by Kinbote after the fact, and so all the events of the novel have been necessarily filtered through Kinbote’s memory.
On page 78, Nabokov (as Kinbote) introduces Gradus into the plot.  He writes:

We shall accompany Gradus in constant thought, as he makes his way from distant dim Zembla to green Appalachia, through the entire length of [Shade’s] poem, following the road of its rhythm, riding past in a rhyme, skidding around the corner of a run-on, breathing with the caesura, swinging down to the foot of the page
